terms.definition: Ability to develop, test, and launch changes quickly, without waiting for physical hardware.
A system remains operational most of the time, even through partial failures (e.g., multiple Availability Zones).
Creating and configuring resources (servers, databases, network) for use.
Command-line interface for administering AWS services with commands.
Libraries for integrating AWS services from application code.
Distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets (e.g., EC2 instances) to improve availability and performance.
Bring Your Own License: using already-purchased software licenses when migrating to the cloud.
Capital expenditure: upfront investment in physical assets (servers, buildings).
AWS framework with 6 perspectives (Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security, Operations) to guide cloud adoption.
Lightweight packaging of an application with its dependencies; shares the host OS.
Running code without managing servers (Lambda, Fargate); AWS handles provisioning.
A technical or resource limit of an AWS service (manageable via Service Quotas).
CDN configuration defining the origin and how content is cached at edge locations.
Ability to grow and shrink automatically with real demand.
A system's ability to handle more load by adding resources (horizontally or vertically).
Adding more instances/machines instead of making one bigger.
A message queue that decouples components and absorbs demand spikes.
Paying for what you consume instead of investing upfront (OpEx).
A key-value pair attached to resources; cost allocation tags allow tracking spend by project or department.
Letting users from an external identity system (company or web) access AWS without their own IAM accounts.
Virtual firewall at the instance level controlling inbound and outbound traffic; stateful.
A policy restricting actions to keep compliance in a multi-account environment.
Infrastructure as Code: defining infrastructure in versioned templates (CloudFormation) to create it repeatably.
Service for centrally managing human access and federation (SSO) across AWS Organizations accounts.
The set of AWS Regions, Availability Zones, and edge locations.
Discount for committing to stable capacity usage for 1 or 3 years.
Spare EC2 capacity with a large discount, but which AWS can interrupt.
The Rehost migration strategy: moving workloads to the cloud without significant changes.
Multi-factor authentication: a second factor in addition to the password.
Granting only the permissions strictly necessary for a task.
An architecture deployed in several Regions for DR, latency, or data residency.
Operating expense: continuous payment for consumed services.
Each of the 6 framework areas: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability.
Publish/subscribe model: a publisher sends messages to all subscribers (SNS).
A geographic area with multiple isolated Availability Zones.
A requirement that data remain stored in a specific geographic location.
Strategies to recover operations after a severe failure (e.g., multi-Region).
Adjusting resource size to real need to optimize costs.
An identity with permissions that is assumed temporarily; ideal for services and applications.
A model where AWS manages the infrastructure; the customer only provides code or data.
A segment of a VPC; it can be public (internet access) or private.
Ability to keep operating correctly even when components fail.
The identity with full account access; must be protected with MFA and used only for tasks that require it.
One or more independent data centers with separate power and networking within a Region.
Optional firewall at the subnet level; stateless with numbered rules.
Authentication for applications (end-user sign-up/sign-in).
Portal to download AWS compliance reports and agreements.
Tracks resource configurations and evaluates compliance against rules.
Audit log of actions and API calls in the account.
The most detailed cost report, delivered to S3.
Tool to visualize, analyze, and forecast spend.
Status of AWS services and events affecting your account.
Centralized management of multiple accounts: consolidated billing, policies, and discounts.
Service to store and rotate secrets such as credentials and API keys.
Managed protection against DDoS attacks.
Best practice recommendations on cost, security, performance, fault tolerance, and service limits.
Web application firewall against common HTTP exploits (SQLi, XSS).
Persistent block volumes for EC2 instances.
Automatically adds or removes EC2 instances according to demand.
Elastic shared file system (NFS) for Linux instances.
In-memory cache (Redis/Memcached) to reduce latency.
Event bus with rule-based routing.
Automated scanning of software vulnerabilities and network exposures.
Object storage with classes by access pattern and 99.999999999% durability.
Publish/subscribe messaging with push delivery to multiple subscribers.
Managed message queues to decouple systems.
A logically isolated private virtual network within AWS.
Protection of stored data (disks, buckets, volumes).
Protection of data while traveling over the network (TLS/HTTPS).
Linking on-premises environments with the cloud (VPN or Direct Connect).
AWS secures OF the cloud (infrastructure); the customer secures IN the cloud (data, configuration, access).
The combination of CPU, memory, network, and storage of an EC2 instance, organized by families and categories.
A spend commitment (USD/hour) for 1 or 3 years in exchange for discounts.
Folder-structured storage shared across instances (EFS, FSx).
Data stored as objects with metadata and URLs (S3); ideal for static files and backups.
Virtual disks attached to instances (EBS); they behave like a hard drive.
A dedicated private link between premises and AWS.
Service Control Policies: policies that limit maximum permissions in member accounts.
Ability to keep critical operations running during interruptions; supported by multi-AZ/multi-Region architectures.
By aggregating the demand of millions of customers, AWS buys and operates at a lower unit cost.
Managing container deployment, scaling, and health (ECS, EKS).
Rules that automatically move or delete objects between storage classes.
A point-in-time backup of an EBS volume (stored in S3).
A CloudFront point of presence for caching content close to users.
A private connection to AWS services without traversing the internet (concept: PrivateLink).
